transcript.content:
I'm trying to determine whether I would be able to see the Moon right now.

I'm in Anchorage, Alaska, USA at 2026-11-30 00:29 AKST (UTC-0900) (2026-11-30T09:29:00Z in UTC), at latitude 61.2181 degrees and longitude -149.9003 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is -50.024 degrees and its azimuth is 353.005 degrees, so it is below the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 10.813 degrees and its azimuth is 86.037 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 59.58 percent illuminated, 100.894 degrees from the Sun, and 372201.8 kilometers away. The sky brightness is night, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Yes—under those conditions, you should very likely be able to see the Moon.

Why:

- **Altitude 10.8°**: The Moon is above the horizon, though fairly low. That is roughly one fist-width held at arm’s length above the eastern horizon.
- **Azimuth 86°**: Look almost due east, slightly north of due east.
- **Illumination 59.6%**: A waxing or waning gibbous Moon is very conspicuous to unaided vision, especially in a dark sky.
- **Sun at −50° / night sky**: It is fully dark, so the Moon should stand out strongly.
- **Clear sky**: This removes the main obstacle, particularly because low-altitude objects are vulnerable to clouds and haze.
- **Moon–Sun separation ~101°**: It is well away from the Sun’s glare; there is no twilight issue.

The main practical caveat is the **low elevation**. At only about 11° up, local terrain, buildings, trees, mountains, haze, or low cloud toward the east could hide it. Anchorage’s surrounding terrain can matter a lot depending on your exact view. Atmospheric extinction and refraction near the horizon will also make it somewhat dimmer and possibly distorted, but a 60%-lit Moon should still be easy to spot if you have an unobstructed eastern horizon.

So: **yes, almost certainly—look low in the eastern sky, about 10–11° above the horizon.**
